bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external

executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for

analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

     1	# MASSCAN: Mass IP port scanner
     2	
     3	This is an Internet-scale port scanner. It can scan the entire Internet
     4	in under 5 minutes, transmitting 10 million packets per second,

     6	
     7	Its usage (parameters, output) is similar to `nmap`, the most famous port scanner.
     8	When in doubt, try one of those features -- features that support widespread
     9	scanning of many machines are supported, while in-depth scanning of single
    10	machines aren't.
    11	
    12	NOTE: masscan uses its own **ad hoc TCP/IP stack**. Anything other than
    13	simple port scans may cause conflict with the local TCP/IP stack. This means you 
    14	need to use either the `--src-ip` option to run from a different IP address, or
    15	use `--src-port` to configure which source ports masscan uses, then also
    16	configure the internal firewall (like `pf` or `iptables`) to firewall those ports
    17	from the rest of the operating system.
    18	
    19	This tool is free, but consider contributing money to its development:
    20	Bitcoin wallet address: 1MASSCANaHUiyTtR3bJ2sLGuMw5kDBaj4T
    21	
    22	
    23	# Usage
    24	
    25	Usage is similar to `nmap`. To scan a network segment for some ports:
    26	
    27		# masscan -p80,8000-8100 10.0.0.0/8 2603:3001:2d00:da00::/112
    28	
    29	This will:
    30	* scan the `10.x.x.x` subnet, and `2603:3001:2d00:da00::x` subnets
    31	* scans port 80 and the range 8000 to 8100, or 102 ports total, on both subnets
    32	* print output to `<stdout>` that can be redirected to a file
    33	
    34	To see the complete list of options, use the `--echo` feature. This
    35	dumps the current configuration and exits. This output can be used as input back
    36	into the program:
    37	
    38		# masscan -p80,8000-8100 10.0.0.0/8 2603:3001:2d00:da00::/112 --echo > xxx.conf
    39		# masscan -c xxx.conf --rate 1000
    40	
    41	
    42	## Banner checking
    43	
    44	Masscan can do more than just detect whether ports are open. It can also
    45	complete the TCP connection and interaction with the application at that
    46	port in order to grab simple "banner" information.
    47	
    48	Masscan supports banner checking on the following protocols:
    49	  * FTP
    50	  * HTTP
    51	  * IMAP4
    52	  * memcached
    53	  * POP3
    54	  * SMTP
    55	  * SSH
    56	  * SSL
    57	  * SMBv1
    58	  * SMBv2
    59	  * Telnet
    60	  * RDP
    61	  * VNC
    62	
    63	The problem with this is that masscan contains its own TCP/IP stack
    64	separate from the system you run it on. When the local system receives
    65	a SYN-ACK from the probed target, it responds with a RST packet that kills
    66	the connection before masscan can grab the banner.
    67	
    68	The easiest way to prevent this is to assign masscan a separate IP
    69	address. This would look like one of the following examples:
    70	
    71		# masscan 10.0.0.0/8 -p80 --banners --source-ip 192.168.1.200
    72	      # masscan 2a00:1450:4007:810::/112 -p80 --banners --source-ip 2603:3001:2d00:da00:91d7:b54:b498:859d
    73	
    74	The address you choose has to be on the local subnet and not otherwise
    75	be used by another system. Masscan will warn you that you've made a
    76	mistake, but you might've messed up the other machine's communications
    77	for several minutes, so be careful.
    78	
    79	In some cases, such as WiFi, this isn't possible. In those cases, you can
    80	firewall the port that masscan uses. This prevents the local TCP/IP stack
    81	from seeing the packet, but masscan still sees it since it bypasses the
    82	local stack. For Linux, this would look like:
    83	
    84		# iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 61000 -j DROP
    85		# masscan 10.0.0.0/8 -p80 --banners --source-port 61000
    86	
    87	You probably want to pick ports that don't conflict with ports Linux might otherwise
    88	choose for source-ports. You can see the range Linux uses, and reconfigure
    89	that range, by looking in the file:
    90	
    91	    /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range
    92	
    93	On the latest version of Kali Linux (2018-August), that range is  32768  to  60999, so
    94	you should choose ports either below 32768 or 61000 and above.
    95	
    96	Setting an `iptables` rule only lasts until the next reboot. You need to lookup how to
    97	save the configuration depending upon your distro, such as using `iptables-save` 
    98	and/or `iptables-persistent`.
    99	
   100	On Mac OS X and BSD, there are similar steps. To find out the ranges to avoid,
   101	use a command like the following:
   102	
   103	    # sysctl net.inet.ip.portrange.first net.inet.ip.portrange.last
   104	
   105	On FreeBSD and older MacOS, use an `ipfw` command: 
   106	
   107		# sudo ipfw add 1 deny tcp from any to any 40000 in
   108		# masscan 10.0.0.0/8 -p80 --banners --source-port 40000
   109	
   110	On newer MacOS and OpenBSD, use the `pf` packet-filter utility. 
   111	Edit the file `/etc/pf.conf` to add a line like the following:
   112	
   113	    block in proto tcp from any to any port 40000:40015
   114	    
   115	Then to enable the firewall, run the command:
   116	    
   117	    # pfctl -E    
   118	
   119	If the firewall is already running, then either reboot or reload the rules
   120	with the following command:
   121	
   122	    # pfctl -f /etc/pf.conf
   123	
   124	Windows doesn't respond with RST packets, so neither of these techniques
   125	are necessary. However, masscan is still designed to work best using its
   126	own IP address, so you should run that way when possible, even when it is
   127	not strictly necessary.
   128	
   129	The same thing is needed for other checks, such as the `--heartbleed` check,
   130	which is just a form of banner checking.
   131	
   132	
   133	## How to scan the entire Internet
   134	
   135	While useful for smaller, internal networks, the program is really designed
   136	with the entire Internet in mind. It might look something like this:
   137	
   138		# masscan 0.0.0.0/0 -p0-65535
   139	
   140	Scanning the entire Internet is bad. For one thing, parts of the Internet react
   141	badly to being scanned. For another thing, some sites track scans and add you
   142	to a ban list, which will get you firewalled from useful parts of the Internet.
   143	Therefore, you want to exclude a lot of ranges. To blacklist or exclude ranges,
   144	you want to use the following syntax:
   145	
   146		# masscan 0.0.0.0/0 -p0-65535 --excludefile exclude.txt
   147	
   148	This just prints the results to the command-line. You probably want them
   149	saved to a file instead. Therefore, you want something like:
   150	
   151		# masscan 0.0.0.0/0 -p0-65535 -oX scan.xml
   152	
   153	This saves the results in an XML file, allowing you to easily dump the
   154	results in a database or something.
   155	
   156	But, this only goes at the default rate of 100 packets/second, which will
   157	take forever to scan the Internet. You need to speed it up as so:
   158	
   159		# masscan 0.0.0.0/0 -p0-65535 --max-rate 100000
   160	
   161	This increases the rate to 100,000 packets/second, which will scan the
   162	entire Internet (minus excludes) in about 10 hours per port (or 655,360 hours
   163	if scanning all ports).
   164	
   165	The thing to notice about this command-line is that these are all `nmap`
   166	compatible options. In addition, "invisible" options compatible with `nmap`
   167	are also set for you: `-sS -Pn -n --randomize-hosts --send-eth`. Likewise,
   168	the format of the XML file is inspired by `nmap`. There are, of course, a
   169	lot of differences, because the *asynchronous* nature of the program
   170	leads to a fundamentally different approach to the problem.
   171	
   172	The above command-line is a bit cumbersome. Instead of putting everything
   173	on the command-line, it can be stored in a file instead. The above settings
   174	would look like this:
   175	
   176		# My Scan
   177		rate =  100000.00
   178		output-format = xml
   179		output-status = all
   180		output-filename = scan.xml
   181		ports = 0-65535
   182		range = 0.0.0.0-255.255.255.255
   183		excludefile = exclude.txt
   184	
   185	To use this configuration file, use the `-c`:
   186

   230	## Comparison with Nmap
   231	
   232	Where reasonable, every effort has been taken to make the program familiar
   233	to `nmap` users, even though it's fundamentally different. Masscan is tuned
   234	for wide range scanning of a lot of machines, whereas nmap is designed for
   235	intensive scanning of a single machine or a small range.
   236	
   237	Two important differences are:
   238	
   239	* no default ports to scan, you must specify `-p <ports>`
   240	* target hosts are IP addresses or simple ranges, not DNS names, nor 
   241	  the funky subnet ranges `nmap` can use (like `10.0.0-255.0-255`).
   242	
   243	You can think of `masscan` as having the following settings permanently
   244	enabled:
   245	* `-sS`: this does SYN scan only (currently, will change in the future)
   246	* `-Pn`: doesn't ping hosts first, which is fundamental to the async operation
   247	* `-n`: no DNS resolution happens
   248	* `--randomize-hosts`: scan completely randomized, always, you can't change this
   249	* `--send-eth`: sends using raw `libpcap`
   250

   258	
   259	This program spews out packets very fast. On Windows, or from VMs,
   260	it can do 300,000 packets/second. On Linux (no virtualization) it'll
   261	do 1.6 million packets-per-second. That's fast enough to melt most networks.
   262	
   263	Note that it'll only melt your own network. It randomizes the target
   264	IP addresses so that it shouldn't overwhelm any distant network.
   265	
   266	By default, the rate is set to 100 packets/second. To increase the rate to
   267	a million use something like `--rate 1000000`.
   268	
   269	When scanning the IPv4 Internet, you'll be scanning lots of subnets,
   270	so even though there's a high rate of packets going out, each
   271	target subnet will receive a small rate of incoming packets.
   272	
   273	However, with IPv6 scanning, you'll tend to focus on a single
   274	target subnet with billions of addresses. Thus, your default
   275	behavior will overwhelm the target network. Networks often
   276	crash under the load that masscan can generate.

   280	
   281	Masscan supports IPv6, but there is no special mode, both are supported
   282	at the same time. (There is no `-6` option -- it's always available).
   283	
   284	In any example you see of masscan usage,

   286	IPv4 and IPv6 addresses simultaneously in the same scan. Output includes

   292	
   293	Instead, you'll probably want to scan large lists of addresses stored
